title: Mary Magdalene (22 July)
hook: the apostle to the apostles now has a full feast day

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cephas: a fisherman and a tentmaker, once at odds, on one feast. Your line was two pillars. Which friend did you thank? Day one thousand forty-six.

Long loose hair, a jar of ointment at her elbow, eyes lifted, sometimes a skull on the table beside her. In some old paintings, that woman is Mary Magdalene, the weeping sinner. It's a powerful picture. But the Gospels don't paint it. They never call her a prostitute. What they do give her is something else entirely: a job. She's sent with a message, and the people she carries it to are the apostles themselves. That's why one of her old titles sounds like a riddle: the apostle to the apostles. Today, Mary Magdalene.

Start with Luke. He introduces her among the women traveling with Jesus: "Mary called Magdalene, out of whom went seven devils." Healed, then. Not a sinner in the text: someone set free. He says these women "ministered unto him of their substance": they paid for the mission out of their own money. When Jesus is crucified, John places her at the cross. And on Easter morning, in John's Gospel, she's alone at the tomb, crying, until the risen Jesus calls her by name and she knows him. Then the part that's easy to skip. He doesn't let her hold on. He gives her an errand: "go to my brethren, and say unto them, I ascend unto my Father, and your Father; and to my God, and your God." And she goes. "Mary Magdalene came and told the disciples that she had seen the LORD, and that he had spoken these things unto her." In John, she's the one who tells them, before Jesus appears to the others that evening. So where did the sinner come from? Over time, some Western preaching merged her with other women in the Gospels: the unnamed woman who weeps on Jesus's feet in Luke, and Mary of Bethany. The texts never join them. Orthodox Christians, who didn't take up that merging, honor her as equal to the apostles. The Catholic Church now keeps her day as a full feast, and uses that old title for her: apostle to the apostles. Different churches, one thing in common. The first words of Easter, in John, travel through her.
screen: `HEALED, NOT A SINNER IN THE TEXT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a woman's witness. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a woman who told you something true that changed things. A grandmother, a teacher, a friend, a nurse, a stranger on a bad day. Maybe someone who wasn't believed at first. Remember what she said, and how she said it. If you pray, you can thank God for her by name, the way the church remembers Mary Magdalene by name. If you don't, just thank her in your mind, and let her words be heard properly this time. The bell holds the time.
Mary Magdalene. Healed and sent, the woman at the tomb who carried the news of Easter to the apostles, remembered with a feast of her own.
Your line: she told them first. Today, when a woman tells you something that matters, give her your full attention, and if it's hers, give her the credit out loud. Day one thousand forty-six.

howItsDone: On Mary Magdalene's day, churches that keep it read John 20's garden scene; the Catholic Church keeps it as a feast, and Orthodox Christians honor her as equal to the apostles.

original.note: Greek: I have seen the Lord. Mary's words in John 20:18, in modern Greek editions.

trapdoor: what you thought: the repentant sinner of the old paintings.
what it means: a woman healed by Jesus, at the cross and the tomb, sent to tell the apostles she had seen the Lord.
what a scholar hears: the sinner image comes from later merging with unnamed women; John makes her the one who carries Easter's first message.

notes: Claims rule: no date is given for the Catholic Church raising her memorial to a feast (2016) or for the Western merging of figures (often traced to Gregory the Great); both are left undated. Confirm 'now keeps her day as a full feast' and 'some Western preaching'.

'The first words of Easter, in John, travel through her' and the carry 'she told them first' rest on John 20:18 preceding 20:19; confirm framing.

Editor pass: 1035 (Sunrise service) already quoted John 20:16 in full, used the gardener scene and Mary's recognition, set a fork on Mary at the tomb, and taught Ῥαββουνί as its original word. To avoid repeating it ten days later: the recognition is now one paraphrased clause (John 20:16 source changed to paraphrase), the teach weight moves to the errand and John 20:18, the match pair 'Rabboni' became 'at the cross', the fork now asks what she tells the disciples, and the original word is now ἑώρακα τὸν κύριον (John 20:18, 'I have seen the Lord'); confirm form and pronunciation. The Rabboni note above no longer applies.

Second editor pass: hook no longer opens 'A woman...' (1039, 1043 and 1045 also open 'A ...'); stock phrases 'Here's the trouble' and 'Here's what the Gospels actually say' replaced with plainer lines.

Audit pass: ἑώρακα τὸν κύριον ('I have seen') is the modern critical text of John 20:18; the Greek behind the KJV reads ἑώρακε ('she had seen'), which is why the KJV quotation is in the third person. Original note now says 'in modern Greek editions'; confirm.
